overarching_question: When should an adaptive tutoring system request executable programming evidence, and how much should it trust the result?

findings.label: External-model benchmark
findings.question: Did requesting executable evidence for every case improve prediction?
findings.result: After correcting the scoring fault, the dialogue-only condition was correct for 18 of 23 eligible cases. Adding the related coding task increased this to 19 of 23.
findings.interpretation: The extra evidence changed one prediction, and unrelated passing evidence performed equally well. This run did not show a practical or relevance-specific advantage.
findings.sample: 23 eligible authored cases; one pinned external-model run per response channel.

findings.label: Bayesian tracker study
findings.question: Can a bounded update reduce harm when evidence becomes unreliable?
findings.result: Across 500 adverse simulated episodes, bounding the update reduced average squared probability error by 0.0094. In the clean setting, the error increased by 0.0033, below the declared 0.0100 limit.
findings.interpretation: The safeguard helped under the declared failures and imposed a small cost when evidence was clean. This is a simulator result, not evidence about real learners.
findings.sample: 500 independent simulated episodes per declared condition.

findings.label: Selective probing study
findings.question: At a fixed 50% budget, did the reliability-aware policy choose better probes?
findings.result: Across six held-out simulated environments, the proposed policy reduced error by 1.19 percentage points against random selection. It was 0.86 points worse than uncertainty-only selection and 0.54 points worse than ordinary value-of-information selection.
findings.interpretation: The proposed policy beat random selection, but it did not beat the stronger simple policies. The planned claim of an overall advantage was therefore unsupported.
findings.sample: 2,000 independent simulated episodes in each of six held-out environments.

findings.label: External learner-record study
findings.question: Did model uncertainty identify predictions that were more likely to be wrong?
findings.result: Selecting the most uncertain half of 729 predictions captured 141 of 195 errors (72.3%). Random selection would be expected to capture 49.5%; the learner-level 95% interval for the difference was 16.4 to 29.0 percentage points.
findings.interpretation: Uncertainty was useful for prioritising review on this historical dataset. The study did not request executable probes or measure whether tutoring improved learning.
findings.sample: 729 predictions from 86 learners across 19 programming problems.

claim_boundary: These studies examine prediction, evidence reliability, and selective evidence collection. They do not show improved human learning, better live tutoring, reduced cognitive offloading, or deployed cost savings.
